But the amendment's limits were built into its text from the start. It forbade denial of the vote on racial grounds — not all voter qualifications. This left the precise gap that Southern states would later exploit: poll taxes, literacy tests, grandfather clauses, and white primaries all operated without ever naming race, yet achieved racial exclusion with surgical precision. The inclusion at the constitutional summit contained the mechanism of its own circumvention.

The amendment did not abolish all voter qualifications; it prohibited racial exclusion. Southern states nevertheless undermined its enforcement: poll taxes, literacy tests, and grandfather clauses used ostensibly race-neutral terms, while white primaries excluded Black voters explicitly. Discriminatory administration could empty the constitutional guarantee of practical force. This was a failure to enforce the prohibition, not constitutional permission to discriminate.

The political mechanism was the exploitation of the precise gap the Fifteenth Amendment left open. The Amendment prohibited denial of the vote on grounds of race — not all voter qualifications. Southern states seized this space: poll taxes, literacy tests, grandfather clauses, white primaries. Not one of these devices named race in its text. Each achieved racial exclusion in its operation.

The political mechanism exploited the distance between a constitutional prohibition and its enforcement. The Fifteenth Amendment prohibited racial exclusion without abolishing all voter qualifications. Southern states used ostensibly neutral poll taxes, literacy tests, and grandfather clauses alongside explicitly exclusionary white primaries. These devices achieved racial exclusion in practice; that did not make the discrimination constitutionally permissible.
